value_chain_position: Multi-country gold/silver producer selling refined dore/concentrate from company-operated mines.
cost_curve_verified: Proxy and company-reported figures AGREE on the direction, and the agreement is unflattering: the deterministic proxy shows a 67.8% trailing-twelve-month margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation but places Fortuna at the very bottom of its eight-name precious-metals cohort on cost, and the company's own 2026 guidance confirms it - consolidated all-in sustaining cost of $1,830 to $1,975 per gold-equivalent ounce (Seguela $1,630-1,730, Lindero $1,520-1,655), with the first quarter of 2026 actually printing $2,107, above the top of the full-year range. The fat margin is a gold-price effect, not a cost-position effect. The one genuine cost-curve strength is mine-level and not consolidated: Seguela's 2025 cash cost was $679 per ounce, and the Diamba Sud feasibility study dated 29 June 2026 carries a $1,056 per ounce all-in sustaining cost over its first four years, which would improve the group's position if built on budget.
gm_trajectory: Margins are rising on flat-to-falling revenue, which is the good version of this pattern. Gross margin went 22.6% (2023) to 32.4% (2024) to 48.7% (2025) while revenue actually fell 9.6% in 2025 to $960 million because two mines were sold; gross profit still rose 36%. On a trailing-twelve-month basis to March 2026 revenue is $1.10 billion (up 7.1% year on year) at a 67.8% margin on earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and free cash flow has gone from negative $57 million (2022) to $81 million, $162 million, $294 million and now $366 million.
bull_thesis: Fortuna is a debt-free, cash-generating gold producer trading at roughly 3.1 times enterprise value to trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, against 6.3 to 8.2 times for Alamos, SSR Mining and Pan American - and it is the rare small-cap miner where management has already proved it will do the right thing with the money. Over the past five quarters it sold its two highest-cost, shortest-life mines (San Jose in Mexico and Yaramoko in Burkina Faso) for $84 million gross plus a $57.5 million pre-closing dividend, avoiding roughly $50 million of future closure spending; took net cash from $137 million to $493 million; issued no equity since 2021; and turned a decade of dilution into real buybacks, retiring 8.6 million shares for $80.2 million at an average $9.32 in the second quarter of 2026 alone, about 2.8% of the company in three months. That is management buying its own stock below where we think it is worth. The operating base is better than the consolidated cost line suggests: Seguela in Cote d'Ivoire produced 152,420 ounces in 2025 at a $679 per ounce cash cost, beat the top of guidance in both 2024 and 2025, and runs its plant 40% above nameplate. On 29 July 2026 the board approved a $109 million, 30% capacity expansion taking throughput from 1.75 to 2.3 million tonnes a year and output above 200,000 ounces annually for a decade, with a payback of about two and a half years. Behind it sits Diamba Sud in Senegal, whose 29 June 2026 feasibility study showed a 60% after-tax return and a one-year payback at $3,500 gold, a $1.009 billion after-tax net present value at a 5% discount rate ($1.287 billion at $4,000), 1.15 million ounces of probable reserves, and - crucially - a $1,056 per ounce all-in sustaining cost over its first four years. The environmental decree arrived 15 June 2026 and the technical report was filed 13 July 2026, meaning the project is permitted on the environmental side, fully engineered, and funded from cash flow with no equity required. If both projects land, Fortuna moves from roughly 293,000 ounces in 2026 to about 500,000 ounces at a materially lower cost, with reserves of 3.0 million ounces (up 15% year on year after depletion, April 2026) plus 2.1 million indicated and 2.2 million inferred behind them. At spot gold of $4,154 an ounce, the current book alone generates roughly $850 million of annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation against a $2.75 billion market value and $466 million of net cash. Conditions that must hold: gold above roughly $3,300; Diamba delivered near its $397.5 million budget and Q2 2028 first-gold date; the Seguela expansion commissioned in the second half of 2028; and no adverse change to the mining codes or state participation terms in Cote d'Ivoire, Senegal, Argentina or Peru.
bear_thesis: You are being asked to pay 3.1 times peak-cycle earnings for a four-country, sub-300,000-ounce producer that has just committed roughly $530 million of growth capital at the highest gold price in history, and the arithmetic of a normal cycle is brutal. The deterministic torque proxy says a 10% fall in gold takes about 14% off earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation - roughly $120 million a year at the current run-rate - and that cuts symmetrically. Take gold from $4,154 to $3,000 an ounce, a level that would still be historically high, and consolidated earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation fall from roughly $850 million to roughly $550 million; against a 2026 capital programme of $330 million rising further in 2027 as Diamba Sud's $397.5 million build, the $109 million Seguela expansion and about $25 million of self-operated underground development all run at once, free cash flow goes negative and the buyback - currently the largest incremental buyer of the stock - stops. The cost picture is already deteriorating in plain sight: consolidated all-in sustaining cost guidance for 2026 is $1,830 to $1,975 per gold-equivalent ounce, and the first quarter printed $2,107, above the range, with management's own explanation (royalties that scale with the gold price, share-based pay that scales with the share price) getting worse rather than better if things go well. Second, the growth story has already slipped roughly a year in the telling - February 2026's '500,000 ounces over the next 24 months' became July 2026's 'toward 500,000 ounces by 2028', and the feasibility study's Q2 2028 first gold plus a second-half-2028 Seguela ramp makes 2029 the first full year at target. Even then, 500,000 ounces only restores the 460,000 gold-equivalent ounces the company already produced in 2024. Third, execution risk is concrete, not theoretical: Lindero missed 2025 guidance by 6% because of crusher failures traced to structural fatigue in the foundations, requiring a 35-day shutdown in March 2026; two contractor fatalities have occurred at Seguela; and the chief executive himself warned in February 2026 that equipment delivery times and skilled labour 'are quickly going to come in high demand and shortage' - which is a description of the cost inflation he is walking into. Fourth, the jurisdictions are the discount: Cote d'Ivoire holds a 10% free-carried interest in Seguela, Senegal takes 10% free-carried plus a 3.5% royalty and a 0.5% social contribution at Diamba with an option on a further 25%, Argentina cost $10 million in currency losses in nine months of 2025, and Fortuna has already been forced out of Burkina Faso and is withdrawing from Mexico. The market is not confused when it prices Fortuna alongside B2Gold at 2.8 times rather than Alamos at 6.7 times. Finally, the long record is a dilution record: weighted shares went from 129 million in 2015 to 309 million in 2024, a 2.4-fold increase, and the buyback has so far bought back less than one year of that history. What would confirm the bear case: gold below $3,300; a Diamba capital estimate revised above roughly $450 million; consolidated all-in sustaining cost staying above $2,000 for a second and third quarter; or the buyback being suspended to fund construction.
sop_bull: Favourable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each asset separately), built at spot gold of $4,154 and silver of $60.17 per ounce holding, with 303 million shares outstanding: Seguela at 90% attributable (Cote d'Ivoire holds 10% free-carried), 200,000-plus ounces a year for a decade post-expansion at about $1,550 all-in sustaining cost, discounted at 9% = $2.6 billion, or $8.60 a share. Lindero at 100,000 ounces a year including the 400,000-ounce target below the current pit floor = $1.0 billion, or $3.30 a share. Caylloma re-rated on $60 silver with access to its high-grade zones = $250 million, or $0.83. Diamba Sud at 85% of the feasibility net present value at $4,000 gold ($1.287 billion), 90% attributable after Senegal's free-carried interest = $984 million, or $3.25. Exploration and investments - the 15% Awale Resources stake, the Quartzstone earn-in in Guyana, Tongon North, Cerro Lindo, Sunbird Deep and 2.2 million inferred ounces = $300 million, or $1.00. Net cash grown to roughly $600 million by year-end = $2.00. Less the capitalised drag of $28-30 million of annual corporate overhead = minus $1.00. Total: about $18.00 per share.
sop_bear: Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the precious-metals cycle turns and gold reverts to $3,000 an ounce (down 28% from spot) with silver back to $35, mid-construction: Seguela at 175,000 ounces and cost creep to $1,850 all-in sustaining cost = $800 million attributable, or $2.65 a share. Lindero at 95,000 ounces with cost creep to $1,800 in an Argentine cost base, discounted at 12% = $300 million, or $1.00. Caylloma barely covers its costs at $35 silver against $31-36 all-in sustaining cost = $60 million, or $0.20. Diamba Sud's net present value falls to roughly $730 million at $3,000 gold; assume a 25% capital overrun (about $100 million) on a West African build into equipment shortages, take the 90% attributable share and apply a 0.45 development discount for a project being constructed into a falling metal price = $250 million, or $0.83. Exploration and investments written down to $50 million, or $0.17. Net cash reduced to about $1.35 a share once the committed Seguela expansion capital and buybacks are honoured. Less the $1.00 corporate overhead drag. Total: about $5.20 per share. Allowing for the fact that a debt-free balance sheet and a company buyback would cushion the decline, the adverse case prices at roughly $5.75 - close to, but below, the $6.17 low of the past year.
sop_fair_value: $10.80 per share (a working range of $10.25 to $11.25)
sop_breakdown: Base case built on a $3,900 per ounce long-run gold price - below the $4,154 spot but above the company's own $3,750 planning assumption - with 303 million shares. Seguela, 90% attributable, 200,000-plus ounces a year post-expansion at about $1,600 all-in sustaining cost, discounted at 9% and adjusted for the two-year ramp: $4.70 a share. Lindero, 97,000 ounces at about $1,590 all-in sustaining cost over a nine-year life, discounted at 12% for Argentine currency and repatriation friction: $1.95. Caylloma, small and short-lived but cash-generative at current silver prices: $0.36. Diamba Sud, feasibility net present value of roughly $1.15 billion at a $3,900 deck, 90% attributable after Senegal's free-carried interest, times a 0.65 development discount for a permitted, funded, feasibility-stage project two years from first gold: $2.21. Exploration and investments - the Awale stake, Quartzstone, Tongon North, Cerro Lindo and 2.2 million inferred ounces: $0.40. Net cash of $466 million verified on the 31 March 2026 balance sheet ($676 million cash against $209 million of total debt including $73 million of leases; the company quotes $493 million on its own definition): $1.54. Less the capitalised drag of $28-30 million a year of corporate overhead: minus $1.06. Total $10.80. That figure implies an enterprise value of about $2.8 billion against roughly $805 million of 2026 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at the same gold deck - about 3.5 times, still well inside the 6.3 to 8.2 times the mid-cap peers command, which is deliberate: the discount pays for four-country political exposure and two simultaneous builds.
risk_reward: At $9.075 the adverse case is $5.75 and the base case is $10.80, so the downside to break is materially larger than the upside to fair value - the asymmetry does not work at this price on a base-case reading. The favourable case of $17.50 is where the reward lives, but it requires two construction projects delivered on time and gold holding near record levels. The level that changes the arithmetic is roughly $7.50, where the base case offers a far wider gap than the adverse case and the buyback is still active.
catalyst_status_note: The events that were supposed to force a re-rating have already happened, in a six-week run, and all are verified from dated company releases: the environmental decree for Diamba Sud from Senegal's Ministry of Environment on 15 June 2026; the feasibility study on 29 June 2026 (60% after-tax return, one-year payback, $1.009 billion net present value at $3,500 gold, first gold Q2 2028); the National Instrument 43-101 technical report filed 13 July 2026 with a 30 June 2026 effective date; and the board's approval of the $109 million, 30% Seguela expansion on 29 July 2026. The share price has not re-rated on any of them - it sits at $9.075 against a 52-week high of $13.85. The remaining dated item is ordinary rather than thesis-changing: second-quarter results after the close on 5 August 2026 with the call on 6 August (announced 23 July 2026). The one genuinely pending approval, Senegal's final mining permit (application filed 4 February 2026), carries no published date and so is not a scheduled event. Per this lane's rules this status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict.
peer_comps_note: On trailing enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, Fortuna trades at 3.08 times against Pan American at 8.24, Alamos at 6.70, SSR Mining at 6.30 and B2Gold at 2.77. The market is grouping Fortuna with B2Gold - the West-Africa-political-risk bucket - rather than with the mid-cap operators. That grouping is half stale and half fair. Stale, because Fortuna exited Burkina Faso in April 2025 and is withdrawing from Mexico; its West African exposure is now Cote d'Ivoire and Senegal, two of the better-functioning jurisdictions in the region. Fair, because Fortuna really is a sub-300,000-ounce producer across four countries with above-average consolidated costs, heading into two simultaneous builds, and it earns a 13.3% free cash flow yield and a 17.1% return on invested capital at a record metal price. Even our base fair value of $10.80 leaves the shares at only about 3.5 times forward enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation - we are not underwriting peer parity, only a partial closing of an unusually wide gap.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is narrower than the bulls would like, and it is a disagreement about which risk is being priced. Coverage here is thin to the point of being unrepresentative: exactly one price target printed in the last quarter, $14.50 from Eric Winmill on 30 July 2026 when the stock was $8.37, against five targets over the past year averaging $11.70. That is not a street-wide view, it is one analyst. Meanwhile Zacks moved Fortuna to its lowest rank on 26 June 2026, which is an earnings-estimate-revision signal rather than a valuation one - and it is mechanically misleading here, because consolidated ounces are 35% below 2024 for the deliberate reason that two mines were sold, so reported per-share earnings estimates read as 'falling' even while free cash flow per share sets records. The specific market assumption we think is wrong: that Fortuna belongs in the same risk bucket as B2Gold at 2.8 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Fortuna exited Burkina Faso in April 2025, is winding down Mexico, and now runs Cote d'Ivoire, Senegal, Peru and Argentina, with a debt-free balance sheet, $466 million of net cash and an entire growth programme funded from internal cash flow. It has also done what almost no small-cap miner does at a cycle peak: bought back 2.8% of itself in one quarter instead of buying somebody else. The specific bull assumption we think is equally wrong: that the 500,000-ounce target arrives in 2028. The feasibility study puts Diamba's first gold in the second quarter of 2028 and the expanded Seguela plant ramping in the second half of 2028, which makes 2029 the first full year at target - and the company's own language has already slid from 'the next 24 months' in February 2026 to 'by 2028' in July 2026. Our conclusion is that both the pessimists and the optimists are wrong by roughly the same margin, which is why we arrive at a fair value only about 19% above the current price rather than at the $14.50 target.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months are the cash-flow trough of this story, and the pressure is on costs rather than solvency. The 2026 capital programme is roughly $330 million with 56% allocated to growth and exploration; from 2027 the $397.5 million Diamba Sud build, the newly approved $109 million Seguela expansion and about $25 million of extra capital to self-operate the Sunbird underground mine all run concurrently. Consolidated all-in sustaining cost in the first quarter of 2026 was $2,107 per gold-equivalent ounce against a full-year guide of $1,830 to $1,975, and the two drivers management named - royalties that rise with the gold price and share-based pay that rises with the share price - both get worse if the thesis works. Lindero took a planned 35-day crusher-foundation replacement in late March 2026 at an estimated $2.2 million, so the second quarter is where that disruption shows. And the torque cuts down as well as up: on the deterministic proxy, a 10% fall in gold removes about 14% of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, roughly $120 million a year at the current run-rate. A move to $3,000 an ounce would take 2026 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation from roughly $850 million to roughly $550 million and push free cash flow negative once both builds are at full spend - at which point the buyback, currently the largest incremental buyer of the shares, would have to stop. The mitigant is the balance sheet: $676 million of cash against $209 million of total debt including $73 million of leases, and no maturity wall. This is a margin-compression and sentiment risk, not a survival risk.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling event waiting here, and that is part of why the setup is unexciting rather than explosive. Fortuna pays no dividend, so there is no yield-focused base to flush. The register is index and quantitative money - Dimensional Fund Advisors raised its stake 5.6% in the first quarter of 2026 to 10.6 million shares - plus a notably retail-heavy gold audience: the May 2025 call included a private investor telling management 'I've been buying all the way down on the sell-off... this is a fantastic deal as I'm concerned', and a newsletter writer promising to continue the conversation on a podcast. A retail-heavy holder base sells on price action, not on mechanics. The one systematic seller is the estimate-revision crowd: Fortuna's move to the bottom Zacks rank on 26 June 2026 is a divestment trigger for a slice of quantitative money, and it is being driven by the optical decline in ounces from the 2025 divestments rather than by any deterioration in cash generation. Pushing hard the other way, the company itself is the marginal buyer of size: 8.6 million shares for $80.2 million in the second quarter of 2026, about 26% of that quarter's cash generation, under a renewed authorisation to repurchase up to 15.2 million shares from 4 May 2026. That is a real, largely price-insensitive bid beneath the stock, and it is why a washout back toward the $6.17 low of the past year would require a genuine move down in gold rather than merely a change in sentiment.
forcing_function: The dated events that mattered have already fired, and the shares did not respond: environmental decree 15 June 2026, feasibility study 29 June 2026, technical report filed 13 July 2026, and board approval of the 30% Seguela expansion on 29 July 2026. The next hard date is second-quarter results after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, with the conference call on Thursday 6 August at 9:00 a.m. - the first print that will show whether all-in sustaining cost is coming back inside the $1,830 to $1,975 guide after the $2,107 first quarter, and whether net cash still built after $80.2 million of buybacks. Beyond that, the genuinely thesis-changing milestones are further out and mostly undated: Senegal's final mining permit, applied for on 4 February 2026 with the environmental decree now in hand; first gold at Diamba Sud in the second quarter of 2028; and the expanded Seguela plant ramping in the second half of 2028, with Sunbird underground mining starting in the second quarter of 2027. In other words, this is not an event trade - it is a two-year execution story, and the honest forcing function is quarterly cash flow delivery rather than any single date.
moderator_conclusion: This is a good company at a fair price, not a good company at a cheap price, and the difference is the whole call. Fortuna has earned genuine respect over the past five quarters: it sold its two worst mines before they became liabilities, refused to buy anything while sitting on $816 million of liquidity at a record gold price, took net cash from $137 million to $493 million, issued no equity since 2021, grew reserves 15% after depletion, and turned a decade of dilution into a buyback that retired about 2.8% of the company in a single quarter at an average $9.32. Every dated promise on Diamba Sud was kept almost to the month, and the resulting feasibility study - a 60% after-tax return, a one-year payback, and a $1,056 per ounce cost over the first four years - would improve where Fortuna sits on the industry cost curve rather than merely adding ounces. That earns the forensic side of the file a high mark. The problem is arithmetic, not character. Valuing the business asset by asset at a $3,900 long-run gold price - below today's $4,154 spot but above the company's own $3,750 planning assumption - we reach about $10.80 a share, roughly 19% above the current $9.075. Price the same assets into a cycle turn at $3,000 gold, mid-construction, with a plausible capital overrun on a West African build, and we reach about $5.75. The downside is bigger than the base-case upside, and the reward case at $17.50 needs two projects delivered on time into the tightest equipment and labour market the gold industry has seen in fifteen years. Two other facts keep us from paying up today. First, the consolidated cost line is drifting the wrong way: 2026 guidance of $1,830 to $1,975 per gold-equivalent ounce with a $2,107 first quarter is not a low-cost producer, whatever the 67.8% trailing margin suggests - that margin is the gold price talking. Second, the headline growth target has quietly slipped about a year in management's own language, from '500,000 ounces over the next 24 months' in February 2026 to 'toward 500,000 ounces by 2028' in July 2026, and even that only restores the 460,000 ounces produced in 2024. So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. We want Fortuna near $7.50, where the gap to fair value roughly doubles and the buyback is still running, or we want the 6 August second-quarter print to show all-in sustaining cost returning inside guidance and net cash building through an $80 million buyback - which would let us underwrite the base case with more confidence and less price cushion. Judged purely on what you get for the money and how clean the numbers are, ignoring timing entirely, this is a strong value case: 3.1 times trailing enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation against 6.3 to 8.2 times for Alamos, SSR Mining and Pan American, 17% of the market value in net cash, a 13.3% free cash flow yield, and a management team buying stock below intrinsic value. The single ingredient that stops it being our highest value rating is that the cheapness rests on earnings struck at the highest gold price in history - a peak-earnings illusion risk we can measure but not eliminate. One discipline worth stating plainly: nothing in this verdict rests on the gold chart. We are judging the miner - its cost position, its reserve life of about ten years at the current run-rate on 3.0 million ounces of proven and probable reserves, its contract-free spot exposure at 95% of revenue, and its capital discipline - and the miner is better than its multiple but not cheap enough, today, to size.
